1:
Whose words these are is asked first. Gill notes that the old versions join them to the close of the previous chapter by supplying a word of saying, and takes them for the speech of the afflicted. Henry allows either the prophet addressing the people or the people addressing one another, and sees him striking while the iron was hot and setting in with the convictions his neighbours seemed to be under; from which he draws the rule that people who went from God in a body ought in a body to return.

Henry lays out the two inducements: their experience of his displeasure, since it was he who tore them, and their expectation of his favour, since he that has torn will heal, as a surgeon binds up with a tender hand the bone he has set. The same providence that afflicts God's people relieves them, he adds, and the same Spirit that convinces the saints comforts them, so that what is first a spirit of bondage becomes a spirit of adoption. Clarke sets the words against the earlier threat: God had said he would tear and go away, and they answer that he has torn but will heal, whereas their allies had torn and given no healing. Wesley says they now see his hand in all they suffer.

Calvin turns the same point into a rule about repentance. Since terror drives men away from approaching God, the prophet adds that the afflictions would not be such as to produce despair. The beginning of repentance is a sense of God's mercy: when men are persuaded that he is ready to pardon they gather courage to repent, and otherwise however much their sin frightens them they will never return. He supports it from the Psalm which says that with God is mercy, that he may be feared.

The two days and the third divide the readers. Gill reports Jewish schemes making them the ruined temples or the successive captivities. Clarke takes the words of the death and resurrection of Christ, and observes that this is the only place in the Old Testament where such a resurrection seems to be hinted at. Ellicott dissents. He reads the verse as the haste of seeming penitents expecting a rapid restoration, and explains that after two days is a phrase sometimes used for tomorrow while the third day means after a short time. He grants that some Christian interpreters, Jerome among them, give the passage sole reference to the resurrection of Christ, but holds with Calvin that this is contradicted by the form of the expression, and calls it far-fetched over-refinement to bring in the resurrection without New Testament warrant.

Calvin agrees, and adds a caution. He allows that the reference to Christ is not unsuitable, since Christ rose as the first-fruits of those who shall rise; yet it seems too refined. We must mind that we fly not in the air, he says, for subtle speculations please at first sight and afterwards vanish, and whoever would make proficiency in the Scriptures should gather only what is solid. He reads the phrase instead as a second consolation, that if God does not revive them at once the delay need not weary them.

The following on to know is read as a promise, not a condition. Gill observes that the word if is not in the original and the sentence is absolute, so that it runs, we shall know, we shall follow on to know the Lord. Keil and Delitzsch describes the knowledge as practical, consisting in keeping the commandments and growing in the love of God. Calvin makes it the exercise of faith in the dark: when God hides his face we act foolishly in cherishing unbelief, since faith is exercised by lifting our eyes to a light that seems extinguished and in the darkness of death still promising ourselves life.
4:
The question God asks himself is felt as a difficulty. Henry calls the expression strange and meets the objection head on: can Infinite Wisdom be at a loss, or put upon taking new measures? By no means; God speaks after the manner of men, to show how unreasonable the people were and how just his proceedings, so that they may not complain of him as harsh for tearing them. From it he draws the rule that God never destroys sinners till he sees there is no other way with them. Clarke states it as a deadlock between two attributes: they had too much goodness for total rejection and too much evil to be placed among the children, so that when justice was about to destroy them it was prevented by their repentance, and when mercy was about to bless them it was prevented by their relapse.

The morning cloud is where the disappointment lies. Henry allows that some take the goodness of their kindness to themselves in repenting, but prefers their piety, which appeared and vanished. In drought the morning cloud promises rain and the early dew is a refreshment, but the cloud is dispersed and the dew drawn back into the air while the earth stays parched; and since what does not continue can hardly be said to have been done, such goodness is neither pleasing to God nor profitable to ourselves. Ellicott renders it as your love to me is like the morning cloud which promises rain and does not give it, and the mist which vanishes in the blaze of summer; and he marks the verse as the point where the language of the supposed penitents ends and Jehovah answers.

Calvin uses the turn to state a canon of reading. Whenever the prophets make known the grace of God, he says, they add an exception, lest hypocrites apply to themselves what is offered to the faithful alone; they never threatened ruin without adding a promise, and never held out a promise without a caution. Having to do at once with the whole people and with the few faithful, they mingled consolations with reproof, and those consolations belong only to the remnant.

The hewing by the prophets is explained from the trade. Gill compares them to lapidaries who cut stone and hewers who cut off knotty parts, saying that by preaching the terrors of the law they cut the people to the heart. Keil and Delitzsch settles the grammar, that the preposition is instrumental rather than meaning among the prophets, and that the prophets meant cannot be false ones because of the parallel phrase about the words of God's mouth; through them God had carved the nation, or as the older translators put it, worked it like hard wood into a holy people. Calvin explains why such treatment was needed. Nothing is more pleasing to God than to deal kindly with us, but our perverseness does not let him follow the inclination of his nature; and when hypocrites expostulate that he declares himself merciful and now fulminates, he answers that they constrained him, since a hard knot needs a hard wedge, and his word, sweet food to the meek, had to be to them an axe.

The last clause is where the text itself comes into question. Clarke reports that the versions generally read my judgment rather than thy judgments, and explains the difference as a single letter wrongly carried from one word to the next; the true reading, he thinks, is that God's judgment goes forth as the light, at once evident and swift. Ellicott reaches the same conclusion independently, saying an error has crept into the received Hebrew text from which the old versions are free, the mistake being an initial letter misplaced as a final one; Wesley alone keeps the received text, of punishments so exactly answering the prediction that anyone might see them.
6:
The preference stated in the verse is carefully qualified. Gill takes it as the one rather than the other, granting that sacrifices were of divine appointment and were types of Christ, but holding that beside the moral duties God did not will them, and that he did not accept at all those offered to the calves at Dan and Bethel. Keil and Delitzsch is more explicit: it is not sacrifices in themselves that are rejected but the heartless sacrifices with which the wicked fancied they could cover their sins, and the love meant is love to one's neighbour rooted in the knowledge of God. Ellicott prefers love to mercy, and cites another saying to show that even by Old Testament measure the moral ranks above the ceremonial, ritual being valueless apart from conformity to the divine will. Wesley explains the two terms, compassion towards men being one principal duty of the second table put for all, and the knowledge of God being that affectionate knowledge which fills the mind with reverence of his majesty and submission to his will.

Calvin treats the verse as forestalling an evasion. Hypocrites never want a cover, and it is their practice to maintain that they worship God so long as they offer sacrifices and accumulate rites, supposing him thereby bound to them. He notes that the Son of God quoted the words twice, once when the Pharisees reproached him for keeping company with men of abandoned life, which showed that God is not worshipped by external ceremonies but where men bear with one another, and once when they blamed the disciples for plucking ears of corn, which showed that those who make holiness consist in ceremonies blame their brethren without cause. He adds that sacrifice and burnt-offering here stand for the whole of external worship. Clarke states the preference more simply, that God was more willing to save than to destroy and would rather see them full of penitent resolutions than offering the best and most numerous victims on his altar.

The comparison in the next verse is disputed three ways. Gill reports that some take it of Adam, who transgressed the covenant of works in paradise, while the Targum makes it the men of old. Clarke argues for the first and says the other is scarcely sense: they sinned against light and knowledge as Adam did, and the similarity is striking, since Adam transgressed in paradise and was cast out, while Israel transgressed in possession of the promised land and was cast out into captivity. Ellicott agrees that the marginal rendering gives the strongest meaning, God having promised Adam the blessings of paradise on condition of obedience, which he broke, as Israel violated the terms on which the goodly land had been given. But he also reports a recent proposal that the name is used in many places for all the other races of mankind as against Israel, those outside the chosen people being called Adam because they are regarded as nothing but his descendants.

Calvin takes the clause another way again. On his reading the transgression of the covenant is the corruption of the worship: God's design in appointing the sacrifices was that there should be nothing carnal in their sacrificing, whereas they corrupted the whole law and were perverse interpreters of it, their sacrifices being mockery, as though it were a satisfaction to God to have an ox killed. He then puts weight on the little adverb that follows. There, he says, is emphatic: it is exactly in their ceremonies that their perfidy is convicted, since they abused the sacred marks by which God had sanctioned his covenant in order to cover their own faithlessness, setting out their sacrifices as though God's mouth could be stopped by that defence. Wesley reads the same word as a place rather than an occasion, in the very land God had given them by covenant.
8:
Why Gilead in particular is named is partly recoverable and partly not. Calvin says at once that the prophet notices something special against the place which the imperfection of history has left obscure to us. What can be said is that Gilead was one of the cities of refuge, held by the Levites, where a man who had killed another by chance could flee and be safe once his case was heard. Gill identifies it with Ramoth-gilead and takes it for all the cities of refuge in those parts, whose priests ought to have known the laws and instead made a trade of sinning. Ellicott is less sure of the identification, inferring a town of the name east of the Jordan distinct from Mizpah; and he renders the second clause more exactly as betrodden, or foot-tracked, with blood, adding that murder in a city of refuge adds to the horror. Clarke supplies a different association, that this was where Jacob and Laban set up the heap of stones called the heap of testimony, and suggests that idolatry was set up there and that perhaps the heap itself became an object of superstitious adoration.

Calvin makes the standing of the offenders the point. The priests ought to have been examples to everyone, since the Lord chose them to carry a torch before the people; so it was monstrous that they should be like robbers and that a holy city, which was as it were the sanctuary of God, should become a den of thieves. He puts the difficulty as a question about where to begin, since if the people were reproved indiscriminately the priests would suppose themselves spared, whereas in fact they were the ringleaders. Wesley says the same shortly, that the inhabitants, though Levites and priests, worked all manner of wickedness.

The figure of the robbers is filled out from ordinary life. Gill describes a gang lying in wait in a ditch or a cave for a man they know will pass with money, and reports another comparison, of fishermen casting in their hooks from the bank. Keil and Delitzsch has them forming into gangs like highwaymen to rob travellers, and notes that the old Greek misunderstood the first half of the clause by confusing two similar words, while Jerome rendered it strangely as well. Clarke gives the sharpest motive: the country was infamous for robberies, the idolatrous priests formed themselves into companies and kept possession of the roads and passes, and if they found anyone going to Jerusalem to worship the true God they put him to death.

One word in the verse divides the readers cleanly. Ellicott renders it as a place: as a robber lies in wait, so the company of priests murder on the road to Shechem; and he notes that Shechem too was a city of refuge and a Levitical city, on the road to Bethel where the priests of the calves resided. Calvin denies this outright. The word properly means the shoulder, he says, and is transferred to the sense of consent, as where a people is said to serve the Lord with one shoulder, meaning with one accord; so here the priests conspire together with consent, and those who think a place-name is intended are much mistaken. Wesley follows the same sense, that the priests by companies lay wait and rob and murder.

Calvin also limits what is being charged. It is certain, he says, that the prophet does not speak of open murders, since it is not credible that Gilead had become a slaughter-house; the prophets simply speak this way whenever they upbraid men with cruelty. What the closing clause shows is that these men were not open robbers, publicly infamous in the sight of men, but robbers before God, since the word rendered lewdness properly means a design and is often taken in the bad sense of a wicked trick.
10:
The horrible thing is identified without difficulty. Gill takes it of the idolatry of the calves at Dan and Bethel, and observes that the word carries the sense of hair standing on end. Clarke says the idolatry had so prevailed that the whole land was defiled, and Wesley dates it from the Ephraimite who brought it in two centuries before. Ellicott adds a detail from the pointing of the text, that the Hebrew punctuation makes the reciter hesitate before pronouncing the horrible thing, which grated through his teeth; and he takes the house of Israel here for Ephraim and Judah together.

Calvin uses the clause to settle who has the right to judge. God declares himself the fit judge of these vices, he says, in order to cut off the vain excuses hypocrites bring when reproved; for they wish their own will to stand for reason, setting up good intention as a queen ruling heaven and earth while God is excluded from his own rights. By a single word, he says, God lays prostrate whatever men set up for themselves: you think this is my worship and in your imagination the most holy religion, whereas I declare it profanation, so that you may take your fopperies elsewhere.

The harvest at the end is read as a threat by some and a promise by others. Gill offers both, a time of wrath and vengeance, which a harvest sometimes signifies, or else a time of joy such as harvest ordinarily is. Clarke takes the severe sense: the harvest would come, the sickle was already thrust in, and what she had sowed she should reap. He prefers a rendering which makes the last clause say among those who lead away the captivity of my people, so that the nations carrying Israel off would carry Judah too; and he grants that from the common reading some take the clause for a promise of return, adding that Judah was indeed brought back but that the greater part of Israel never returned. Wesley keeps the kind sense, that Judah should not be cut off as Israel was, but a seed of her sown and reaping with joy. Ellicott sides with the severe reading, calling it a harvest not of joy but of sorrow, in contrast to the usual gladness of the season when the Feast of Tabernacles was kept; he thinks the last clause is best joined to the chapter following, and reports that some derive the word rendered captivity from a different root and give it the sense of destiny.

Calvin objects to the received construction on grammatical grounds. Interpreters render the clause as though Judah had set a harvest for herself, but the verb is plainly in the third person; and those who take it in the second, to mean that Judah prepared a miserable harvest by sowing ungodliness, reach that sense only by straining. Since the word means a plant as well as a harvest, he takes it so here, of Judah propagating her own impieties. On his reading the complaint is that the defection of the ten tribes had not destroyed religion altogether, the pure worship remaining at Jerusalem in outward form, but that Judah was now planting shoots of her own, and doing so at the very time when God was seeking to restore the scattering of his people. He closes with a figure from medicine: one who undertakes the cure of a diseased body and finds some parts still whole has hope of a remedy, whereas here no part was whole.

Keil and Delitzsch reads the mention of Judah structurally, brought in at the close so that Judah should not think itself less culpable than Israel; and he settles the subject by elimination, since Israel would supply no thought in keeping with the connection and Jehovah is himself the speaker, so that the verb has to be taken passively.
